Chapter 7: Negotiating With Pop Culture — Joy, Critique, and the Search for Better Stories
Pop culture is always there, isn’t it? It’s with us on our morning commute, in our group chats, and humming in the background as we go about our day. For a lot of us, it brings real joy—a sense of connection, a way to find common ground and make sense of what’s happening in the world around us.
But let’s be honest—if you’re someone who also notices its flaws, that relationship can feel a bit complicated.
Picture this: a group of friends getting together for a movie night, eager to see the latest romantic comedy. The jokes get some good laughs, the chemistry is fun to watch, but when the credits roll, someone in the group points out the same old patterns. You know, the quirky best friend who never gets her own story, the total lack of queer characters, or how the heroine’s happiness seems to depend on a guy.
The group laughs it off, maybe shrugs, and starts a debate: can you really enjoy something, yet still wish it was better?
Somewhere else, a parent and child are curled up together, watching a superhero show. The kid is all about the action, the bright costumes, the wild possibilities. But the parent? They notice how the female characters barely get any screen time, or how almost everyone looks the same.
Still, sharing the story means something. It’s a reminder that even imperfect stories can bring people closer.
Most folks don’t realize just how much pop culture shapes what we expect—from love, to beauty, to what it means to belong. The shows and movies we watch? They become the stories we tell ourselves. And for anyone who rarely sees themselves on screen, that silence can sting—it’s a quiet nudge about who really matters.
But here’s something important: critiquing pop culture doesn’t mean you have to walk away from it. Lots of us learn to hold both joy and disappointment at the same time. We celebrate what works, call out what doesn’t, and keep hoping for better—without giving up the pleasure these stories bring. Some people even become creators, determined to shake things up, tell new stories, and make room for more voices.
Over time, it becomes clear—pop culture isn’t set in stone. It can change. It does change, even if it’s slow. New voices break through, diverse stories find big audiences, and people push for more representation. Every step forward matters, even when it feels like progress is hard won.
So if you love pop culture, here’s the real challenge: stay in the conversation. Enjoy what’s good, call out what needs work, and support stories that make space for everyone. There’s a whole world of stories out there, and there’s room for more.
The hope is simple, but powerful: that someday, everyone will see themselves on screen—not as a sidekick, not as a token, but as a real, complex human being.
